🇱🇧 Zawtar’s Flag and Washington’s Deal: One State, Two Kinds of Courage

Joseph Aoun just became the first Lebanese president at the White House since 2009, arriving with a US‑brokered framework that ties a ceasefire and phased Israeli withdrawal to the verified disarmament of Hezbollah and other armed groups and the restoration of full state sovereignty. 

The June 26 text commits Lebanon to bringing all weapons under state control and deploying the army “up to the Israeli border,” while Israel keeps troops in occupied areas until that disarmament is certified.

In Washington, Aoun struck a maximalist note: Hezbollah can be disarmed, he said, if “occupation” ends, the army controls all territory and reconstruction is run solely by the state — “one state, one army and one security decision.” 

At the White House he thanked Trump for a framework whose “ultimate objective” he framed as ending the state of hostility with Israel permanently. Trump responded with flattery, promised direct US–Lebanon flights and even said he’d talk to Hezbollah if Aoun wanted him to.

On the ground, the pilot looks modest. The army has moved into three zones — Zawtar al‑Gharbiya, Froun and Srifa — but only Zawtar has seen an actual IDF ground pullback; the other two remain under Israeli observation and fire control without permanent forces. 

In Zawtar, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and the defense minister arrived with armored vehicles, planted the Lebanese flag and told residents to stay away until the situation stabilizes — a village Hezbollah ran before the war, which Israel then took by force and is now handing over, cautiously.

Hezbollah’s answer is explicit. Deputy leader Naim Qassem has rejected the disarmament plan and the government’s timeline as a surrender that serves Israel, warning that “any hand that reaches out to take the weapons will be cut off.” 

Aoun keeps talking about dialogue and a weapons monopoly for the state; Hezbollah keeps saying its arsenal is non‑negotiable and tying any flexibility to guarantees and full withdrawal. 

Between them sits an army that has gained operational authority south of the Litani but still avoids the group’s core strongholds for fear of civil war.

And in the same week Beirut sells “one security decision” to Washington, the justice system shows where the state can act fast — and where it can’t. 

Prosecutor Ahmad Rami al‑Hajj has ordered the arrest of journalist Hasan Illaik over a social‑media post criticizing Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, accusing him of harming relations with Riyadh. 

Protesters outside the Palace of Justice demand free expression while denouncing normalization with Israel; a Hezbollah MP calls the case selective enforcement driven by external pressure. 

If you take Aoun’s slogan seriously, Zawtar shows what “one state, one army, one security decision” looks like at the edge of the map. Hasan Illaik’s case shows what it looks like in Beirut. 

The real test of the US‑Lebanon framework is whether a state that handcuffs journalists over tweets will ever dare to test that power on Hezbollah’s guns.
